questions.stem: An annuity PRIMARILY addresses which financial risk?

opts.x: The risk of the breadwinner dying prematurely.
The risk of outliving one's savings.
The risk of property loss from fire.
The risk of the employer failing to pay wages.

questions.answer: (B) The risk of outliving one's savings, receiving income for longer than savings can sustain.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

Longevity risk, the risk of outliving accumulated financial resources, is the defining risk that annuities are designed to eliminate. By converting a lump sum into a guaranteed lifetime income, the annuity ensures the annuitant receives income for as long as they live. The insurer pooling the longevity risk across many annuitants achieves the same statistical predictability that underpins all insurance.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) Premature death risk is addressed by life assurance, the product category designed to provide a lump sum or income to dependants in the event of the breadwinner's early death. Annuities protect against the opposite risk (living too long).
(C) Property fire risk is a general insurance exposure, wholly separate from the retirement income risk that annuities address.
(D) Employer wage default risk (non-payment of contractual wages) is an employment law matter, addressed through the labour courts, not an insurable retirement income risk.

questions.stem: Under PRA 2014, minimum total CPS contributions are:

opts.x: 8% from employee only.
10% from employer only.
18% aggregate: minimum 10% employer + 8% employee.
25%, all from employer.

questions.answer: (C) 18% in aggregate: minimum 10% employer + minimum 8% employee.

why.h: Why (C) is Correct

PRA 2014 Section 7 establishes two separate contribution obligations: the employer must contribute at least 10% of monthly emoluments and the employee at least 8%, giving a combined minimum of 18%. Both amounts are credited to the employee's individual RSA. Employers may voluntarily contribute above 10% (many larger employers contribute 12–15%), but neither may go below the statutory minimum.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) 8% from the employee alone ignores the employer's mandatory 10% contribution, it describes only half the obligation.
(B) 10% from the employer alone ignores the employee's mandatory 8% contribution.
(D) 25% all from the employer has no basis in PRA 2014; the combined rate is 18%, split between employer and employee.

questions.stem: The RLA in Nigeria is regulated by:

opts.x: PenCom only.
CBN only.
NAICOM (financial soundness and product) jointly with PenCom (benefit administration).
Federal Ministry of Finance.

questions.answer: (C) NAICOM (financial soundness and product) jointly with PenCom (benefit administration).

why.h: Why (C) is Correct

The RLA sits at the intersection of insurance and pension regulation. NAICOM regulates the life insurer writing the annuity, its capital adequacy, RBC compliance, NIIRA 2025 product approval, and actuarial solvency. PenCom regulates the RSA transfer process (the mechanics of moving funds from the PFA to the insurer), the PenCom Approved RLA Insurer Register, and the overall benefit adequacy framework that ensures the annuity meets the 50% minimum pension threshold. Both regulators' requirements must be met for a valid RLA to be issued.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) PenCom alone cannot regulate life insurance products; it has no NIIRA 2025 mandate over insurer solvency or product pricing.
(B) CBN regulates banking and monetary policy; it has no direct role in life insurance or annuity products (though it regulates bank treasury functions that may hold RSA assets).
(D) The Federal Ministry of Finance sets fiscal policy but does not directly regulate insurance or pension products.

questions.stem: Under the Nigerian RLA, the 10-year guaranteed period means:

opts.x: The retiree pays premiums for 10 years before receiving income.
If the retiree dies within 10 years, the present value of remaining guaranteed payments is paid to the named beneficiary.
The monthly payment is fixed for 10 years only.
The annuity income increases 10% annually for the first decade.

questions.answer: (B) If the retiree dies within 10 years, the present value of remaining guaranteed payments is paid to the named beneficiary.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

A guaranteed payment period means the annuity is paid for a minimum of a defined number of years regardless of the annuitant's survival. If the annuitant dies within the 10-year guarantee window, the insurer pays the present value of the remaining guaranteed payments (or continues the payment stream, depending on the policy design) to the designated beneficiary. This protects against the 'bad luck' scenario of dying very shortly after purchasing an annuity and receiving almost nothing for a large purchase price.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) Describes a premium payment period before income begins; the opposite of what a guarantee period means. The RLA pays income from inception; there is no waiting period for premium accumulation.
(C) The annuity continues for the lifetime of the annuitant after the 10-year period; it does not stop at 10 years.
(D) A 10% annual income increase describes an escalation feature, a separate and optional product add-on, not the guaranteed period concept.

questions.stem: NIIRA 2025 specifically excludes RLA business from which licence category?

opts.x: Full conventional life licence.
Non-life licence.
Standalone Insurtech licence.
Partnering Insurtech licence.

why.h: Why (D) is Correct

NIIRA 2025 expressly excludes Retirement Life Annuity business from the Partnering Insurtech licence because Partnering Insurtechs are technology/distribution companies; they cannot assume insurance risk on their own account. The long-duration, actuarially complex nature of annuity liabilities requires the full capital adequacy, actuarial governance, and solvency framework applicable to conventional licensed life insurers. Allowing under-capitalised Partnering Insurtechs to assume annuity risk would create material policyholder protection risk for retirees who have converted their lifetime savings.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) Conventional life insurance licence holders are expressly permitted to write RLA business; they have the required capital, governance, and actuarial framework.
(B) Non-life licences cannot write any life or annuity business at all; the exclusion of RLA from non-life is automatic and obvious.
(C) Standalone Insurtech licensees at the life capital level (₦1bn minimum) may write life insurance and are generally permitted to write RLA business, subject to meeting NAICOM's specific RLA requirements.

questions.stem: A CPS retiree who chooses an RLA:

opts.x: Can switch back to PW at any time.
Can only transfer to another RLA provider after at least 2 years; cannot return to PW.
Receives variable monthly payments linked to fund performance.
Must wait 12 months for the first payment.

questions.answer: (B) Can only transfer to another RLA provider after at least 2 years; cannot return to PW.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

The RLA is an irrevocable purchase. Once the RSA has been transferred to the life insurer and the annuity has commenced, the retiree cannot return to Programmed Withdrawal. The decision is final. A transfer between RLA providers (if dissatisfied with service) is possible but requires PenCom and NAICOM approval and is subject to a minimum holding period of approximately 2 years. This irrevocability is the product's primary protection design feature; the insurer can only price and guarantee lifetime income if it can reliably match long-duration assets against the lifetime liability.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) The RLA cannot be switched back to PW at any time; this is precisely why the PW-RLA decision requires careful financial guidance.
(C) RLA income is fixed (or escalating at a defined rate); it is not variable or fund-linked. Variability is the characteristic of Programmed Withdrawal (which depends on fund performance), not the RLA.
(D) The first monthly payment typically commences within 30 days of fund receipt, not after a 12-month waiting period.

questions.stem:
Ngozi, aged 62, has an RSA balance of ₦25 million at retirement. Her last monthly salary was ₦480,000. Use an annuity factor of 8.0 and an expense loading of 5%.
(a) Calculate the minimum residual RSA balance required after the lump sum withdrawal, based on the 50% minimum pension threshold.
(b) Calculate:
(i) the maximum lump sum;
(ii) the residual RLA premium; and (iii) the estimated monthly RLA income.
(c) If Ngozi instead chooses PW with the full ₦25 million, explain the key risks she bears relative to the RLA option.

model.h: Part (a): Minimum Residual RSA Balance

PenCom's 50% minimum pension rule: the monthly RLA income must be at least 50% of the retiree's last monthly salary.

Minimum monthly income required: 50% × ₦480,000 = ₦240,000 per month.

Working backwards: what RLA premium is needed to deliver ₦240,000/month?
Annual income required: ₦240,000 × 12 = ₦2,880,000
RLA premium (before expense loading, using annuity factor): ₦2,880,000 × 8.0 = ₦23,040,000
With 5% expense loading: ₦23,040,000 ÷ 0.95 = ₦24,252,632

Minimum residual RSA balance required for RLA: ₦24,252,632
Part (b): Lump Sum and Monthly Income Calculations

(i) Maximum lump sum:
Maximum lump sum = Total RSA balance − Minimum required for RLA
₦25,000,000 − ₦24,252,632 = ₦747,368

Conclusion: Ngozi can withdraw at most ₦747,368 as a lump sum, barely 3% of her RSA. The 50% pension rule is the binding constraint.

(ii) Residual RLA premium:
₦25,000,000 − ₦747,368 = ₦24,252,632

(iii) Monthly RLA income:
Net premium for annuity (after 5% expense loading): ₦24,252,632 × 0.95 = ₦23,039,999
Annual income: ₦23,039,999 ÷ 8.0 = ₦2,880,000
Monthly income: ₦2,880,000 ÷ 12 = ₦240,000 per month (= exactly 50% of last salary, as required by the minimum pension rule)
Part (c): Key Risks if Ngozi Chooses Programmed Withdrawal

1. Longevity risk: This is the dominant risk. Under PW, the RSA fund must sustain Ngozi's income for however long she lives. At age 62, a Nigerian woman in the formal sector has a life expectancy of approximately 20+ years (to age 82+). If the PW fund is drawn down at ₦240,000/month, the fund would last approximately 17 years at a nil investment return, meaning Ngozi could outlive her savings by her late 70s or early 80s.

2. Investment risk: PW fund performance depends on the PFA's investment returns. In a poor investment environment, the fund grows more slowly, reducing the sustainable withdrawal period.

3. Management complexity: PW requires Ngozi to actively manage withdrawal rates and monitor fund performance over decades, a significant cognitive burden in retirement, particularly if health deteriorates.

4. Inflation risk: PW withdrawal amounts are not guaranteed to keep pace with inflation. If Ngozi maintains a fixed ₦240,000/month withdrawal, inflation will progressively erode its real purchasing power.

RLA advantage: The RLA eliminates all of these risks, income is guaranteed for life, unconditional on investment performance or fund balance.

questions.stem: Distinguish between an immediate and a deferred annuity. Explain how the CPS functions as a deferred annuity system during the working years. Describe PW and RLA as modes of accessing CPS retirement benefits and compare them across income certainty, investment risk, longevity risk, and estate benefit.

model.h: Immediate vs Deferred Annuity

Immediate annuity: Income commences immediately (or within one payment period) following the purchase. The RLA is an immediate annuity, the retiree purchases with their RSA funds and the first payment arrives within 30 days.

Deferred annuity: The benefit purchase or funding occurs now, but income commences at a future date (typically retirement age). During the deferral period, contributions accumulate at an agreed rate or in an investment fund, growing into a larger pot that will eventually produce income.
The CPS as a Deferred Annuity System

Throughout an employee's working life (typically 20–35 years of RSA contributions), the CPS functions economically as a deferred annuity accumulation system:
• Each monthly contribution (18% of emoluments) is invested in the RSA by the PFA.
• The fund grows through investment returns over the accumulation phase.
• At retirement, the accumulated RSA balance represents the deferred annuity purchase price.
• The retiree then 'annuitises', converting the accumulated RSA into either an RLA (guaranteed lifetime income) or PW (managed drawdown).

This two-phase structure (accumulation then decumulation) precisely mirrors the economic structure of a deferred annuity, though administered through separate regulated institutions (PFA for accumulation, life insurer for RLA decumulation).
PW vs RLA Comparison

Income certainty:
• RLA: Guaranteed lifetime income, fixed amount (or defined escalation). Certainty is complete, income is unconditional.
• PW: Variable, monthly amount is recalculated based on fund balance and remaining life expectancy. Falls as the fund diminishes.

Investment risk:
• RLA: Borne entirely by the insurer. The retiree's income is unaffected by investment performance.
• PW: Borne by the retiree. Poor PFA investment returns reduce the sustainable withdrawal period.

Longevity risk:
• RLA: Borne by the insurer. Income is paid for life, no risk of outliving the fund.
• PW: Borne by the retiree. If the retiree lives longer than the fund can sustain, income ceases.

Estate benefit:
• RLA: Residual RSA fund is converted to the annuity purchase price at inception. On death, no residual fund passes to the estate (except where a guarantee period or joint life option applies).
• PW: The residual RSA balance at death passes to the named beneficiaries, the PW retiree preserves an estate benefit.

questions.stem: Explain the actuarial concept of the annuity factor. Discuss why annuity mortality tables use lighter rates than life assurance tables and explain the implications of this adverse selection phenomenon for an insurer writing both life assurance and annuity business in Nigeria.

model.h: The Annuity Factor

The annuity factor (a_x) is the present value of a series of future payments of ₦1 per year (or per month) payable from a given age x until death. It combines two variables:

1. Mortality: The probability of surviving to each future age (derived from the annuity mortality table, which shows how long annuitants are expected to live).
2. Interest: The discount rate (the expected return on assets matching the annuity liability).

Formula: a_x = Σ v^t × ₜp_x
where v = 1/(1+i), the discount factor; ₜp_x = probability of surviving t years from age x.

A higher annuity factor means more expected future payments, either because the annuitant population is expected to live longer (lighter mortality) or because the discount rate is lower (lower investment return assumption).

Practical use: The monthly annuity income = Annual RLA income = (RLA purchase price × (1 − expense loading)) ÷ annuity factor ÷ 12.
Why Annuity Tables Use Lighter Mortality Rates

Annuity tables are based on the observed mortality of the annuitant population, people who have purchased annuities. This population is systematically different from the general population and from the life assurance insured population:

1. Health selection: People who believe they are in good health and expect to live a long time are more likely to purchase annuities (to maximise the return on their purchase price). People in poor health are less likely to annuitise, they prefer lump sum alternatives to preserve estate value.

2. Socioeconomic selection: Annuity purchasers tend to be wealthier, better-educated, and more financially sophisticated than the general population. Higher socioeconomic status correlates strongly with longer life expectancy in Nigeria and globally.

Result: Annuitants live longer than the general population at the same age, requiring lighter (lower) mortality rates in the annuity pricing model to avoid systematic underpricing.
Implications for a Dual-Book Insurer in Nigeria

An insurer writing both life assurance and annuities faces opposite selection dynamics:

• Life assurance book: Anti-selection pressure, higher-risk individuals (those who expect to die sooner) disproportionately seek and maintain high life cover. The life book's mortality experience is heavier than the general population table.

• Annuity book: Positive selection pressure, longer-lived individuals disproportionately annuitise. The annuity book's mortality experience is lighter than the general population table.

Theoretical natural hedge: An insurer holding both books has a partial natural hedge, excess mortality in the life book (increasing life claims) coincides with lower annuity costs (fewer annuity payments for the shorter-lived annuitants), while longevity in the annuity book (more annuity payments) coincides with better-than-expected life assurance experience (fewer death claims).

Practical limitation in Nigeria: The two books may not be sufficiently large or closely correlated to provide an effective hedge. The Nigerian life assurance book is predominantly younger (25–45) working adults; the annuity book is exclusively retired individuals (60+). Their mortality drivers are different and may not move in offsetting directions. Each book must therefore be managed with adequate reserves on its own assumptions.

questions.stem: PenCom data shows a persistent 3:1 preference for Programmed Withdrawal over the RLA. Critically evaluate the factors driving this preference and assess whether it represents an informed financial choice or a failure of consumer protection. Discuss steps that PenCom and the insurance industry should take to improve the quality of the PW-RLA decision for Nigerian retirees.

model.h: Thesis

The 3:1 preference for Programmed Withdrawal over the Retirement Life Annuity partly reflects rational consumer preferences (estate benefit, control, reversibility) and partly reflects consumer protection failures (inadequate pre-retirement guidance, distrust of insurers, and the irrevocability psychology). The combination produces a systematic under-annuitisation that leaves a significant proportion of Nigerian retirees with material longevity risk they have not adequately priced.
Rational Factors Behind PW Preference

1. Estate benefit: PW preserves the residual RSA balance for heirs. In a culture with strong family financial obligation norms and where the retiree may be the principal family wealth holder, the desire to leave an inheritance is powerful and rational.

2. Irrevocability aversion: The RLA cannot be reversed. Committing a lifetime's savings to a single insurer, irrevocably, is psychologically difficult, particularly for a generation that has watched Nigerian insurers fail to pay claims.

3. Distrust of life insurers: Nigeria's insurance industry's claims non-payment history creates a rational basis for preferring a PFA (pension regulator-supervised) drawdown over entrusting lifetime income to an insurer. The trust deficit that limits voluntary insurance purchase also limits voluntary annuity purchase.

4. Inflation concern: A fixed monthly RLA income loses real value to Nigeria's chronic high inflation. Retirees who experienced 30%+ inflation in the 1990s are reasonably sceptical of a fixed-income product over a 20-year retirement.
Consumer Protection Failures

1. Inadequate pre-retirement guidance: Most CPS members approach retirement without having received structured financial guidance on the PW-RLA decision. The default is PW by inertia, not by informed comparison.

2. Point-of-decision complexity: At the point of retirement, retirees are making a once-in-a-lifetime, irrevocable decision often within weeks of leaving employment. The cognitive load at this point (combined with emotional stress, health concerns, and family pressure) is enormous. Without a qualified adviser, the 'safer' choice (PW, more familiar, reversible in principle) wins by default.

3. Longevity underestimation: Nigerian retirees systematically underestimate their remaining life expectancy. A 62-year-old woman in the formal sector has a realistic expectation of living to 80+. Most retirees do not internalise this and therefore do not appreciate the magnitude of the longevity risk they are retaining under PW.
Recommended Improvements

For PenCom:
1. Mandatory pre-retirement counselling: Require every RSA holder within 2 years of planned retirement to attend a structured financial guidance session (not necessarily individual advice, but a qualified group education programme) covering the PW-RLA comparison with personalised illustrations.
2. Mortality transparency: Provide every retiring member with their estimated life expectancy at their current age, combined with a calculation of the probability that PW funds will be exhausted before death.
3. Annuity-default option: Consider a regulated default; the retiree must actively choose PW rather than the RLA. This 'nudge' design has significantly increased annuitisation rates in comparable markets (UK, Chile).

For the insurance industry:
1. Inflation-linked RLA options: Develop and market indexed annuity products where income rises annually with a defined measure, addressing the most commonly cited rational objection.
2. Claims payment transparency: Publish annuity payment track records, years of on-time monthly payments with zero defaults. This is the most effective trust-building action available.
3. Guaranteed period extension: Offer longer guarantee periods (15–20 years) to reduce the estate-loss objection by ensuring most retirees' families receive material benefit even if death is early.

questions.stem: NIIRA 2025 excludes annuity business from Standalone Insurtech licences. Critically evaluate this exclusion's regulatory rationale. Discuss whether the exclusion forecloses valuable innovation; and identify how Insurtechs can legitimately participate in the RLA market without underwriting the annuity risk.

model.h: Thesis

The exclusion of RLA business from Standalone Insurtech licences reflects sound regulatory risk management: annuity liabilities are long-duration, complex, and irreversible for policyholders; the risk profile is fundamentally incompatible with the lower capital and regulatory requirements of the Insurtech licensing track. However, the exclusion does not foreclose Insurtech innovation in the RLA market; it simply defines the appropriate regulatory boundary for who bears the risk.
Regulatory Rationale for the Exclusion

1. Capital mismatch: An RLA purchased with a ₦25m RSA creates a liability of up to 25 years of monthly payments. The present value of this liability is ₦24–26m at inception. A Standalone Insurtech life licence requires only ₦1bn minimum capital. For an Insurtech writing 1,000 RLAs at an average purchase price of ₦20m, the aggregate liability is ₦20bn; 20× the minimum capital. The capital requirement for a meaningful annuity book must be substantially higher.

2. Actuarial complexity: Annuity pricing and reserving requires sophisticated mortality modelling, interest rate duration matching, and longevity stress testing. This demands a level of actuarial governance (Statutory Actuary, annual actuarial investigation, ORSA stress testing) that the Insurtech licence framework, designed for simpler, shorter-duration products, does not fully mandate.

3. Consumer protection priority: For a retiree who has converted their lifetime RSA savings into an annuity, there is no second chance. An insurer that becomes insolvent after accepting a retiree's ₦25m does catastrophic, irreversible harm. Annuity underwriting must be backed by the highest tier of capital, governance, and regulatory oversight.
Does the Exclusion Foreclose Valuable Innovation?

No: the exclusion is precisely calibrated. It excludes Insurtechs from underwriting the annuity risk (bearing the liability for lifetime income payments) but does not exclude them from the RLA ecosystem. Technology-driven innovation in RLA distribution, comparison, and education does not require the Insurtech to be the risk carrier.

The most valuable Insurtech contributions to the RLA market lie in:
1. Comparison and quotation platforms, enabling retirees to compare RLA quotations from multiple NAICOM-approved insurers in real time.
2. Digital onboarding, streamlining the RSA-to-RLA transfer process (currently paper-heavy and slow) through API-connected digital workflows.
3. Education and guidance, delivering accessible financial guidance on the PW-RLA decision at scale through mobile apps, WhatsApp, and USSD channels.
None of these requires the Insurtech to bear annuity risk.
Legitimate Insurtech Participation Pathways

1. Partnering Insurtech model: An Insurtech (with a ₦10m Partnering Insurtech certificate) can act as the digital distribution arm of a fully licensed life insurer writing RLAs. The Insurtech handles: the retiree's PW-RLA comparison journey; the quotation request to multiple insurers; the digital application; the document collection. The risk sits entirely with the licensed insurer.

2. PFA technology partnership: Insurtechs can build technology for PFAs, the system through which retiring RSA holders first engage with the decumulation decision. A well-designed PFA digital platform that presents the PW-RLA choice clearly and enables seamless RLA application to multiple approved insurers could significantly improve annuitisation rates without the Insurtech bearing any insurance risk.

3. Actuarial analytics partnerships: Insurtechs with data science capabilities can provide mortality analytics, longevity scenario modelling, and pricing support to licensed RLA insurers, commercial services that improve the quality of RLA pricing without requiring an insurance licence.
